items.title: Very Interesting Data ! It is often assumed that traders with larger capital have better chances of making money in F&O. FY26 data shows an interestin...
items.description_html:
Very Interesting Data !

It is often assumed that traders with larger capital have better chances of making money in F&O. FY26 data shows an interesting picture.

Among traders deploying less than ₹10,000, 90% were loss making.

This gradually declined as capital increased:
- 86% of traders deploying ₹1-5 lakh made losses
- 76% in the ₹5-10 lakh category
- 68% among those deploying ₹10 lakh-₹1 Cr

For traders deploying more than ₹1 Cr, 36% were loss making.

So larger capital did appear to improve the probability of being profitable.

But there is another side to the data.

The average loss per trader increased sharply with capital deployed - from just ~₹5,500 for traders below ₹10,000 to ~₹3 lakh for ₹1-5 lakh traders & ~₹10 lakh for those deploying ₹10 lakh-₹1 Cr.

For traders deploying more than ₹1 Cr, the average P&L was a staggering loss of ~₹2.6 Cr per trader.

So having more capital may improve the odds, but it clearly does not eliminate the risks of F&O trading.

One important caveat - findings for categories with a relatively small number of traders, particularly Majorly Options Sellers & Futures Traders, should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size.

items.title: I have a different opinion on this order against the two entities supposedly involved in the cas auction manipulation. The outrage seems to be about t...
items.description_html:
I have a different opinion on this order against the two entities supposedly involved in the cas auction manipulation.

The outrage seems to be about this:
Placed buy orders at highest possible point or sell at lowest possible point (3% higher or lower) and that is bad

Because of that the cas equilibrium price spiked

They cancelled those orders

They benefited from options positions in the index

My opinion is on the first two, as I'm not sure how established the others are without their defense.

In the cas it is only sensible to place limit buy orders as high as you can or sell as low as you can. Watch the cas today also, you will find that most orders and quantities are people buying at obscenely high prices or selling at obscenely low.

This is how it should be. Those are limit orders and are designed be executed only at the equilibrium price not at the obscene price.

Now te reason is simple. It's the way orders are filled in the cas.

Every buy order at the highest price is obviously also a buy order at any price below that.

When they match orders, after market buy and sell orders cancel each other out, the remaining orders are like that. Lowest price sell orders will be matched against the highest price buy orders. Once that's done the next set are matched and so on.

To have buy orders at the highest possible price means you're first in the queue after market.orders, but you get the equilibrium price.

The equilibrium price is determined somewhere in the middle by relatively smaller players who place orders, but because of the skew or orders at the extreme ends of the order book it is possible they don't get any fills. That's ok and a teething problem

The regulator might want to tone down the accusation that placing buy orders 3% above ref price is bad. No, it's the only way to try and guarantee execution.

Cancellations are not good after a point...hong kong disallows cancellations in the last few minutes and we should too.

The rest we should wait for a final order. (Podcast on cas coming soon!)

Yicai: "China’s central and local authorities have released a slew of new policy initiatives to try and combat the worrying slowdown in investment growth. Fixed asset investment fell 6.7% in the first seven months of 2026, with private investment tumbling 9.4%."

We seem to be seeing the acceleration of a 10-15 year trend in which economic activity increasingly shifts from the hard-budget constrained parts of the economy (for which the private sector is a rough proxy) to soft-budget constrained parts.

János Kornai's central insight was that a soft budget constraint changes behavior precisely because firms no longer have to treat losses as a binding signal. If an enterprise expects that the government will ultimately refinance or rescue it, the relationship between expenditure and expected return is undermined.

The result, Kornai argued, is likely to be a rising debt burden, excessive investment, weak price responsiveness, and rising inefficiency.

items.title: RT James Broughel: Can you regulate an AI agent that nobody owns, nobody runs, and nobody can be sued for? My new post takes up a fascinating essay by...
items.description_html:
RT James Broughel
Can you regulate an AI agent that nobody owns, nobody runs, and nobody can be sued for? My new post takes up a fascinating essay by @tylercowen and Sonia Farrell Pearson on whether "untethered" agents (their term for AI systems whose actions can't be traced to any legally accountable person) could be governed by making them hold capital, the way banks do.

https://jamesbroughel.substack.com/p/operation-chokepoint-for-ai-agents

The essay has a tension at its center, and to the authors' credit they more or less concede it. You can't impose a punishment on an abstract piece of computer code. Their answer is that capital requirements never apply to the agent directly. They apply to everyone the agent does business with, like compute providers, payment processors, and other counterparties. An unregistered, uncapitalized agent becomes, in a maritime analogy borrowed from @srajagopalan, like a stateless vessel that every port can refuse.

In other words, this is chokepoint regulation. That term carries political baggage. Operation Choke Point and its crypto sequel used bank supervision to squeeze lawful businesses that regulators simply disliked. But the defect there was the target, not the technique. When there's no owner to fine and no body to jail, the intermediary may be the only door the law can knock on.

The capitalization proposal has a clear enforcement problem. Agents with a reason to evade official channels will mostly be able to, so the rules bind the agents that were already inclined to operate in the legitimate economy. I argue this is less damning than it sounds. Fake identities and empty shell companies pose the same problem today, and we judge those legal regimes based on whether they improve behavior at the margin, not on perfection.

Most likely, capitalization is a solution for semi-tethered agents, the ones that still need lawful infrastructure. If fully untethered agents become common, they may be unreachable by this policy — and most others.

Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

El Niño and its impact on the global energy system

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a record high for the time of year, causing forecasters to predict a very strong El Niño will form in the final months of 2026.

Surface temperatures averaged about 29.6°C last week, up from 26.6°C at the same time last year, according to data from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Temperatures were 1°C higher than the previous record for the time of year and 2.7°C above the long-term seasonal average, indicating exceptional warmth across the region.

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific are a key driver of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, the single largest influence on weather patterns at seasonal scale worldwide.

ENSO has significant impacts on the energy production and consumption – including hurricane formation in the Atlantic, winter temperatures and heating demand in the United States, and hydroelectric generation in South America ...

items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

The pandemic didn't just accelerate ecommerce adoption. It helped kill the business model Meesho was built on.

Meesho started noticing more users creating reseller accounts but shipping orders to just their own address.

"Every month, the share of people who were coming and buying only for themselves was going up,” according to co-founder and CEO Vidit Aatrey.

This wasn't the case earlier. But the pandemic had taught consumers how to shop online. They no longer needed a reseller to build trust.

Meesho's leadership went to consumers' homes and heard the same thing repeatedly. The signal became clear.

"If we were slow to adapt to this change, we may not be relevant,” according to Aatrey.

That’s when Meesho pivoted from reselling to a direct consumer marketplace.

More in the latest episode of Legendary Pivots, our series in collaboration with SeedToScale by Accel.

items.title: The story told in this graph is important. If you set a GDP growth target and you cannot get consumption to grow faster than the target, then you also...
items.description_html:
The story told in this graph is important. If you set a GDP growth target and you cannot get consumption to grow faster than the target, then you also cannot allow investment to grow more slowly than the target except to the extent that a rising trade surplus takes up the slack.

By the late 2010s China was already worried about excess manufacturing capacity and the private sector was cutting back on manufacturing investment.

But the collapse in property investment after 2021 changed all of that. In order to keep overall investment from slowing, the authorities forced a massive increase in manufacturing investment whose purpose was not to satisfy unmet demand but rather to balance the decline in property investment.

The consequence shouldn't have been nearly as surprising as it was for many: excess manufacturing capacity exploded into the problem of involution. But as involution forces down the growth rate of manufacturing investment, even as the growth rate of consumption continues to lag, this leaves China with three possible outcomes:

1. Miss the GDP growth target, which is what has been happening in recent momths, but this is probably politically unacceptable.

2. Increase non-manufacturing investment, although with property investment still declining, this basically means more infrastructure investment. I expect this will happen in the second half of 2026, but given that China already so much excess capacity in infrastructure, it isn't east to find investment projects that aren't value-destroying in the aggregate. As one of my academic friends said jokingly last week, thank god for the terrible rainstorms.

3. Run ever larger trade surpluses.

The arithmetic is pretty easy to set out. China must get investment growth to slow sharply, perhaps even to go negative, if it has any hope of reining in debt, but there are only two ways this can happens.

One way is with a surge in consumption growth that balances the slowdown in investment growth by enough to meet its long-term 4% growth target, but this seems unlikely, at best. The other way is without a surge in consumption, which means allowing GDP growth to drop.

Until then, we can think of the growing trade surplus as effectively a residual consequence of the attempt to rein in debt (i.e. non-productive investment) without reducing GDP growth.


Brad Setser: China's current economic malaise in a nutshell -- rising investment in manufacturing can no longer offset the fall in investment in real estate.

The absolute level of investment in manufacturing is still absurdly high. But it is now shrinking not growing.

items.description_html:
RT Data For India
More than one-third of India's manufacturing workforce today, or 23 million workers, is female.

Some states have a higher share of women in the manufacturing workforce proportionate to men. In Telangana, and in northeastern states like Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur, over half of manufacturing workers are women.

Odisha, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh are also close to parity between genders. Meanwhile, Delhi, Haryana and Goa have some of the lowest shares of women in manufacturing.

In most parts of the country, the majority of women in manufacturing work in textiles and apparel. However, there are a few exceptions. Tobacco manufacturing, specifically bidi-making, is the second largest employer of women in manufacturing after apparel, and is concentrated in a handful of states like West Bengal, Telangana and Odisha.

items.description_html:
It's not going to be easy to defend IT in a world that has a) traditionally charged by headcount and b) have inertia because their clients continue to need them for tasks that need humans to own them for blame or responsibility targeting purposes

That second use case will remain, but won't need as much headcount, and AI does take over some tasks well. However there are serious issues because AI gets away with saying sorry i screwed up, which doesn't help, so the blame taking thingy needs people or organizations to ante up.

There are ways of course. Deploying open source models and owning token costs can be an avenue for a cash rich IT co. Security is a huge game changer, and fortification is going to need much more IT plus blame taking. AI has issues when it retrains on output that Ai itself produces which means fixing AI output will be in demand at some point.

Whatever it does AI will result in more jobs, worldwide. It may not be in IT, it may be in areas that seemed impossible with AI.

Penicillin might have seen a massive jump in productivity, but we never stopped making more drugs , delivery technologies or researching more. The light bulb was replaced by the LED eventually, and the light makers that evolved to do more than lights, survived

Intel gave up its semiconductor memory business to Japan in the 70s. And moved to processors. It was a jump that caused enormous internal concern. The Macintosh came in at a time when the Apple 2 was thriving. Each company cannibalized itself to survive. The IT companies that will build on things that threaten their core franchise, the headcount billing, will be the survivors and thrivers tomorrow. It isn't entirely imaginable what that will be, but you can bet on one thing: life funds a way.

It also means this: the winners of yesterday will not be the winners of tomorrow. But we know that. It wasn't Satyam. It wasn't JP associates. It wasn't Kodak. It wasn't Nokia. Someone else won when we thought some of these were likely to stay winners for a long time. But all of these areas created new jobs and new companies thrive in them.

If you think the end of film photography created less jobs for camera people you would be right. But today everyone is a camera person, and the camera created a job for a shopowner who can receive money through UPI with a qr code scanned by a mobile phone camera. There were five innovations in there that killed some job role or the other (qr, mobile, upi) but they all created new jobs.

If the idea is that the current IT companies are hosed, there is that argument. But there will be survivors and thrivers and they might not even be called IT companies eventually.

items.title: RT Nithin Kamath: I've spoken many times about the need to make it easier for NRIs to invest in India. Finally, some great news. SEBI just released a ...
items.description_html:
RT Nithin Kamath
I've spoken many times about the need to make it easier for NRIs to invest in India. Finally, some great news. SEBI just released a consultation paper proposing a fully digital onboarding process for NRIs, without needing them to be physically present in India! Kudos to SEBI for this pragmatic move.

This is huge because NRIs tend to have large amounts of capital to invest and are a highly durable source of inflows into Indian markets. At @Zerodha, we have over 50,000 NRIs investing with us today. A stat that surprised me when we looked at our numbers: ~80% of them are active. That's a ridiculous number. They tend to invest more, take a longer-term view, and seem to be much stickier investors than regular investors.

This number has grown a lot over the last few years, mostly because the process got simpler. SEBI's earlier changes meant NRIs no longer needed the whole PIS setup to invest. Most NRIs now come in through NRO Non-PIS accounts. These accounts work almost like resident accounts today, with intraday, BTST, and F&O access, and no CP code needed.

But one massive bottleneck has remained: onboarding.

Even today, to open an account digitally, an NRI has to be physically in India. If they are abroad, there's a ton of physical documentation involved and dealing with international courier delays. It has always been the most painful part of the journey.

SEBI’s proposals in the new consultation paper fix this longstanding gap. They’re proposing allowing e-signs directly from the client's country of residence. If finalized, this would relax tedious documentation rules and delays. Something that would take 2-3 weeks or even months could be done within 1-2 days. That's a big win. By removing all this friction, this investor base can easily be many times larger.

Getting foreign money into India matters. It helps the investors, but it also helps the rupee and the larger India story. Anything that makes it easier for this money to come into India is worth doing.

items.description_html:
Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) have now reached 31,000 cr. per month. Of course, everyone's bored of listening to us in the Mutual Fund Industry saying that it's good, but bear with me.

The main reason an SIP is useful is not because it "averages" out the entry price over time in a volatile up and down market. That is just something we as an industry decided is a good thing - but it's an outcome, not a goal.

The main reason is: most of us earn money monthly. End of story. You earn, you spend, you save, you invest. That cycle happens monthly, and therefore you SIP monthly.

But the secondary reason is also: if you don't invest it, you probably will spend it. This is why SIPs make sense - you invest first and spend later, usually. So you end up spending only what's left with you, and that "forced" investing of sorts helps you build wealth for later.

Many of us have the discipline to do an SIP manually every month - otherwise called "lumpsum" investing. This is also fine, and probably better because some months you will have way more money, and some you will be on kadki mode.

Disciplined investing initially works because you save the money, not because it grows. The growth happens in later years. So in the first few years, it's mostly your money, your savings that built your wealth. It's in later years that the incremental savings are very small compared to the corpus you have, so your portfolio grows more because of returns rather than because of what you're saving.

Save a little more every month or every year, and you'll build wealth faster. But building wealth isn't the goal, really, for you. We, as mutual funds, help you build wealth, but your story has three parts:
Part 1: You save and invest your money
Part 2: The money grows because of returns
Part 3: You spend the money

Don't forget part 3. Your wealth doesn't define you. Your life does. Make your life better. SIP is a way to help you, but you have to do Part 3 all by yourself. And that, bro, is the best part of it all.

items.description_html:
RT Anchit Gupta
This is a very understandable and well-meaning concern, but I think it misses why display flying exists in the first place.

For an Air Force, attracting high-quality young men and women is a permanent operational requirement. Aircraft, technology and doctrines change, but the institution must continually persuade another generation to choose an unusually demanding profession.

Flying displays have historically been one of the most powerful ways of doing that. In interviews with veterans across generations, I have repeatedly heard versions of the same story: a young boy watched an aircraft display, saw a fighter at close quarters, or encountered the Air Force pilot at an air show, and decided that this was what he wanted to do with his life.

And that is why display teams should not really be viewed simply as “mascots”. They are among an Air Force’s most visible ambassadors. They bring military aviation before people who may otherwise never encounter it, demonstrate precision, discipline, teamwork and professional excellence, and help create the fascination from which future pilots, engineers and airmen emerge. Most major air forces maintain such teams for much the same reason.

The fact that some of the finest pilots are selected is also not incidental. Display flying is extremely demanding, and its credibility rests precisely on the standards of those who perform it. Every possible precaution is taken, but aviation can never be made entirely risk-free. The occasional tragedy, however painful, cannot by itself become the argument for abandoning an activity that has inspired generations to enter the service.

Dhali’s loss was a terrible one. But I would be cautious about framing it as a life lost for an air show. He was performing a recognised professional role within the Air Force, one that has contributed for decades to recruiting, outreach and the public connection with military aviation.

items.description_html:
Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China."

What Xinhua chose not to mention in its article, but what nearly everyone else will focus on, is that Chinese banks recorded a net decline of 340 billion yuan in new yuan loans in July, well below already-low expectations for a 120-130 billion increase.

But while the sharp and unexpected decline in lending in July will get most of the attention from analysts and the press, what is much more important to me is that total social financing, the best proxy for total debt, actually grew quite strongly in July, by 1.4 trillion yuan.

This highlights what we have been seeing all year, which is that China's financing activity is undergoing a structural shift, with the economy relying more than ever on state-led borrowing – and less than ever on private-sector borrowing – to support growth.

items.title: Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either inc...
items.description_html:
Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either increase investment or boost domestic consumption. With the marginal returns on traditional infrastructure and real estate investment severely diminished, the only sustainable path is to increase household consumption. This requires profound structural reform. The ultimate goal of such reform is to transfer wealth and income share from the state and corporate sectors to households."

This is increasingly becoming how most Chinese economists understand the Chinese economy, although only recently have they been so public about it. The key point here (and one with which many Chinese economists still disagree) is that with marginal returns on most investment so low, reducing China's trade surplus through an increase in investment will only make the longer-term adjustment worse.

China, in other words, should be reducing investment, not raising it, in order to regain control over misallocated capital and surging debt, but this also means that the only way to rebalance domestically and reduce the trade surplus requires that saving declines even faster.

Li Wei lists one of the ways the saving share of GDP can decline, by transferring income share from the state and corporate sectors to households in order to boost consumption growth relative to the growth in production.

He is right, of course. This is certainly one way to reduce saving and bring the trade surplus down, but it won't be easy because doing so will undermine China's manufacturing competitiveness.

Unfortunately, there is only one other alternative, and it is much worse. The reduction in saving can also occur with a sharp fall in production growth. As production declines faster that consumption, the saving share automatically declines.

Historically this has been how most countries with a similar problem have been forced to adjust, mainly because, like China, they postponed boosting consumption growth for far too long and instead doubled down on their high-investment-growth model.

Beijing, of course, will want to do everything it can to avoid this form of adjustment, but the longer it postpones adjustment by boosting consumption growth, the more likely the Chinese economy will adjust through a fall in production growth.

items.description_html:
RT ANI
#WATCH | Delhi: On the impact of the US tariff bill on the Indian economy, Chief Rating Officer at CareEdge Ratings, Sachin Gupta, says, “It will have a multi-order impact on the Indian economy. First of all, we have yet to see how the US implements it, because there is a lot of back-and-forth that happens with many of these US regulations. But assuming that there is indeed a 100% tariff levied, we can analyse this impact at two or three levels. One is the most direct impact, which will be on US imports or Indian exports…if there is indeed a 100% tariff, it becomes unviable…if Russian crude oil supply is excluded from the overall global crude market, where total global crude demand is around 100 million barrels a day, with the Strait of Hormuz accounting for 20 million barrels and Russia accounting for about 9 million barrels, of which India and China take roughly 75% and if both India and China decide not to import from Russia at all due to these 100% tariffs, removing up to 30% of global supply will cause a significant impact. While crude prices have recently been relatively benign at around $70 to $85 a barrel, if this scenario becomes a reality, prices could easily go beyond $100 or even $110 to $120 a barrel, causing India's current account deficit to easily more than double from last year's levels strictly on account of crude. Furthermore, at $110 to $120 a barrel, the government would have to pass on those price rises to the fuel pumps, creating a secondary inflationary impact across the broader economy…”

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.description_html:
Creative Newtech has done an interesting acquisition, transforming from a distributor to a manufacturer of an integrated surveillance technology platform.

Creative Newtech has approved the acquisition of 100% of Infinova (India) for up to US$4 million, marking a strategic shift beyond distribution into surveillance technology manufacturing.

The acquisition brings Infinova's India operations, brand rights, technical expertise, experienced workforce, and local assembly & manufacturing facility, providing Creative Newtech with immediate execution capabilities.

More importantly, the deal lays the foundation for a 'Make in India' surveillance platform, enabling the company to build proprietary products, strengthen after-sales support, and reduce dependence on third-party distribution.

The transaction also accelerates Creative's transition from a distribution-led business to an integrated, technology-led surveillance solutions provider, giving it greater control over manufacturing, product ownership, and margins.

The company holds all the relevant licenses from Gem, BIS, and STQC, enabling it to access the government portal. STQC shifts 22% market share from Chinese to Indian brands

This is more than an acquisition—it is a business model transformation, positioning Creative Newtech to move up the value chain from distributing surveillance products to designing, assembling, and manufacturing them under a 'Make in India' strategy.

Creative NewTech trades at 18 PE vs Prizor Vtech 42PE vs Aditya Infotech 110PE
